entry.title: Interview by Radboud Educational Clips
entry.content:
I had the opportunity to contribute to a new online course from Radboud University, in which I was interviewed to discuss the use of AI in health counselling. The interview drew on my PhD research, exploring how AI tools can be applied to the field of mental health care.

Aimed at decision-makers in the sector, the course “Verantwoord omgaan met AI in de GGZ” provides an interdisciplinary framework for the responsible integration of AI in practice. It is available in Dutch here: https://www.ru.nl/radboud-centrum-sociale-wetenschappen/cursussen/al-het-aanbod/cursus-verantwoord-omgaan-met-ai-in-de-ggz

entry.title: Publication at Ethics and Information Technology

link.title: Publication at Ethics and Information Technology

entry.content:
Our paper “Autonomy-supporting chatbots: Endorsing volitional behavior change” has been accepted and published at Ethics and Information Technology Journal. In this paper, we have proposed a theoretical framework for designing chatbots that respect users’ autonomy while supporting them in making health and lifestyle choices.

Read the paper at https://doi.org/10.1007/s10676-025-09877-8

Title

Autonomy-supporting chatbots: Endorsing volitional behavior change

Abstract

Artificial intelligence (AI) applications have become more pervasive, and can have a myriad of effects on society. This has raised discussions regarding their potential ethical consequences. One application of AI is to help people improve their lifestyle choices and engage in positive behavior change. In the design of such applications, it becomes important to recognize the potential impact that they can have on human autonomy. Human autonomy is a widely discussed topic across various fields of AI applications. It is essential to recognize that human autonomy is a complex concept that requires a nuanced understanding of diverse individuals and their levels of volition. Overall, we argue that chatbots, in the domain of health and lifestyle choices, need to incorporate a capacity to communicate with users about their goals, intentions and reasons for making certain choices, and suggest a way of doing that.

entry.title: Interview by NRC Newspaper
entry.content:
I am excited to have been featured in the Wetenschap (Science) section of NRC, a major national newspaper in the Netherlands. The piece was also subsequently picked up and republished by Leeuwarder Courant, a regional newspaper based in Friesland.

In the interview, I had the chance to share our key insights and findings from my PhD dissertation on the development and evaluation of engaging chatbots for health counselling and the controlled use of large language models. We discussed the potential risks when people rely on AI chatbots for health support and the importance of developing safer, more reliable digital tools. I explained our approach of combining the structure and safety of pre-programmed responses with the engaging, natural language capabilities of large language models (LLMs), while still maintaining human oversight. In our research, we found that responses generated by models like GPT-4 were often rated higher in quality than those written by humans, although some generated utterances were deemed inappropriate and required to be filtered out. I also emphasized the need to use these technologies in a supportive way alongside human care, rather than as standalone solutions, and discussed the broader potential of this method in various fields where both engagement and reliability are critical.

Many thanks to NRC and Ellen de Bruin for bringing attention to our research and giving this topic a platform.

Read the full news article, titled “ChatGPT gebruiken als therapeut? Ik zou het niet aanraden”, on the NRC website in Dutch: https://www.nrc.nl/nieuws/2025/12/14/chatgpt-gebruiken-als-therapeut-ik-zou-het-niet-aanraden-a4913854.

entry.title: Defending my PhD Dissertation
entry.content:
I am thrilled to share that I successfully defended my dissertation, titled “Responsible and Healthy Conversations: Developing and Evaluating Engaging Chatbots through Controlled Use of Language Models”, which marked the completion of my PhD studies in the Behavioural Science Institute at Radboud University.

Reaching this meaningful milestone was made possible by the exceptional guidance and support of my supervisors, Prof. Dr. Tibor Bosse, Dr. Iris Hendrickx, Prof. Dr. Emiel Krahmer, and Prof. Dr. Gert-Jan de Bruijn, and the wonderful collaboration with my project partners Linwei He and Divyaa Balaji. I am deeply grateful to all of them!

Special thanks to the members of my thesis committee, Dr. Serge Thill, Prof. Dr. Walter Daelemans, Prof. Dr. Koen Hindriks, Dr. Charlotte Van Hooijdonk, Dr. Mariët Theune, and Prof. Dr. Elisabeth André, for their valuable time and thought-provoking questions.

entry.title: Lecture at SIKS Course: AI & Human Behaviour

link.title: Lecture at SIKS Course: AI & Human Behaviour

entry.content:
I was invited to give a lecture and workshop as part of the AI & Human Behaviour course at the SIKS graduate school. During my talk, I discussed the developments in conversational agents, with a particular focus on the development and evaluation of engaging long-term chatbots designed to support users in health behaviour change, which was the central theme of my PhD dissertation and the Look Who’s Talking project. We went on to explore the potential benefits and challenges associated with applying large language models in medical contexts, along with considerations around their controlled use. The workshop component provided me with an opportunity to demonstrate the usage of our hybrid chatbot development software, HyLECA, followed by the audience members attempting to design and create their own chatbots based on the software’s architecture. Overall, it was a valuable experience to contribute to this multidisciplinary exploration of AI’s role in behaviour change, and to engage with other researchers in the area interested in the technical, ethical, and societal implications of these rapidly evolving technologies.

The two-day course focused on the intersection of artificial intelligence and human behaviour, specifically exploring how AI technologies can support individuals in voluntarily changing their behaviours across domains such as health, sustainability, and justice. The aim of the course is for the students hear from experts in the field about key technological components of AI-based behaviour support systems and engage in assignments related to these technologies. The program also features real-world examples of AI applications, particularly in health and sustainability, and concludes with an examination of how to promote behaviour change in ways that respect and uphold fundamental societal values such as liberty, autonomy, and social justice.

You can find the course details and full agenda at: https://siks.nl/activities/activities/siks-course-ai-and-human-behaviour/

entry.title: Organizing NLG in the Lowlands 2025
entry.content:
I had the pleasure of being one of the organizers of this year’s NLG in the Lowlands workshop, which took place on June 19, 2025, in Tilburg, The Netherlands. NLG in the Lowlands is an informal workshop that has been held for the past several years, providing a venue for researchers from The Netherlands, Belgium and Germany to exchange ideas and share their work on Natural Language Generation and related topics. This year, the workshop was focused on Multimodality and Large Language Models, and featured invited talks, poster presentations, and opportunities for open discussion.

One personal highlight was presenting findings from our human evaluation studies during the poster session. It was great to connect with others working in the same area and get feedback on our work.

You can see the full program of the event on: https://sites.google.com/view/nlg-in-the-lowlands-2025/
entry.summary: I was one of the organizers of NLG in the Lowlands workshop where researchers from the Netherlands, Belgium, and Germany came together to exchange ideas and share their work on Natural Language Generation and related topics.

entry.title: Presentation at Etmaal 2025
entry.content:
I was delighted to discuss the controlled usage of large language models for health-promoting chatbots with the communication science community at this year’s Etmaal van de Communicatiewetenschap. During my talk, I introduced our hybrid chatbot development framework, HyLECA, developed within the Look Who’s Talking project, and shared key findings from our human evaluation studies exploring the use of large language models in chatbot for health, which can be read on this link and this link.

The Etmaal van de Communicatiewetenschap conference is an annual event that brings together communication scholars from the Netherlands and Belgium. This year, the conference was organized by the Department of Communication Science at KU Leuven in cooperation with Netherlands-Flanders Communication Association (NeFCA) on February 3-4 in Bruges, Belgium.
entry.summary: I had the chance to discuss our hybrid chatbot development framework and share insights from our human evaluation studies on using large language models in health-promoting chatbots at ETMAAL 2025.

entry.title: Publication and Presentation at COLING2025
entry.content:
Our findings on the question How well can LLMs reflect? through a combination of extensive human evaluations and experimentation with various prompting strategies, has been published in the main proceedings of the 31st International Conference on Computational Linguistics. The publication also gained a spot in the conference for an oral presentation, which is going to take place on January 21, 2025, in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates.

Read the paper at https://aclanthology.org/2025.coling-main.135.pdf

Title

How Well Can Large Language Models Reflect? A Human Evaluation of LLM-generated Reflections for Motivational Interviewing Dialogues

Abstract

Motivational Interviewing (MI) is a counseling technique that promotes behavioral change through reflective responses to mirror or refine client statements. While advanced Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate engaging dialogues, challenges remain for applying them in a sensitive context such as MI. This work assesses the potential of LLMs to generate MI reflections via three LLMs: GPT-4, Llama-2, and BLOOM, and explores the effect of dialogue context size and integration of MI strategies for reflection generation by LLMs. We conduct evaluations using both automatic metrics and human judges on four criteria: appropriateness, relevance, engagement, and naturalness, to assess whether these LLMs can accurately generate the nuanced therapeutic communication required in MI. While we demonstrate LLMs’ potential in generating MI reflections comparable to human therapists, content analysis shows that significant challenges remain. By identifying the strengths and limitations of LLMs in generating empathetic and contextually appropriate reflections in MI, this work contributes to the ongoing dialogue in enhancing LLM’s role in therapeutic counseling.
